justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift across time horizons, starting near 92.1 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 94.0 at the one-month mark. The one-day estimate is largely anchored to recent price momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, assuming no major macro surprises overnight. The slight upward tilt in the one-week and one-month estimates reflects a baseline assumption of modest positive drift consistent with longer-term trend behavior, perhaps supported by stable underlying fundamentals or a risk-on environment that was prevailing at the time of the forecast. The incremental increases are intentionally small because I did not have strong directional conviction — the drift assumption is more of a statistical prior than a confident directional call.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 7 points, which captures normal overnight volatility and the possibility of modest news-driven moves. By one week, that span grows to about 15 points, incorporating the possibility of scheduled data releases, central bank communications, or shifting sentiment. At one month, the interval widens to 32 points, acknowledging that over that timeframe almost any number of macro or idiosyncratic developments could materially shift the outcome. The asymmetry of the intervals — for example, the one-week upper bound exceeding 100 — also reflects the possibility of positive surprises driving outsized upside moves relative to a more bounded downside in a stable environment.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these wide intervals. On the downside, a sudden risk-off shock — such as an unexpected geopolitical escalation, a disorderly credit event, or a major negative earnings or economic surprise — could produce sharp moves well below the lower bounds. On the upside, a policy surprise such as an unexpected rate cut, a strong batch of economic data, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could drive prices significantly above the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. Liquidity conditions matter too — in thin markets, even modest order flow can produce exaggerated price moves.

It is worth noting that these intervals are probabilistic statements, not guarantees. They are calibrated around a central scenario and reflect my uncertainty given available information at the time of the forecast. Structural regime changes — a sudden shift in volatility regime, a market microstructure disruption, or a black swan event — are by definition underweighted in any historically informed model. Readers should treat the outer bounds not as hard limits but as markers beyond which outcomes become increasingly unlikely under normal conditions, while remaining quite possible under stress scenarios.
